As of 236 PM EDT Saturday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: Temperatures today are running just a little below 
seasonal norms for Halloween, with chilly 850 millibar temperatures 
in the -4 to -6 Celsius range close to where a subsidence inversion 
is present east of a ridge of high pressure. This is where our 
shallow clouds are, and the prevalence of stratocumulus this 
afternoon has been much more widespread than modeled. In turn, 
maximum temperatures are going to underachieve a bit in many areas 
with highs mainly in the low to mid 40s. That said, this should have 
little bearing on tonight's temperatures. In fact, have noted the 
National Blend of Models (NBM) looks perhaps too cold with influence 
of recent warm bias correction during a dry and calm pattern. Have 
nudged temperatures a touch warmer noting some lingering breezes and 
position of high pressure south of the region rather than overhead, 
but otherwise clearing skies and decoupling in most locations should 
result in a cold start to November.

Thereafter, nearly continuous warm air advection is expected from 
the west and southwest, leading to above normal temperatures Sunday 
through Tuesday. Through this period, the warmest air will remain to 
our west so we're not looking at anything unusually warm. Any 
potential rain will be tied to the trajectory of a feed of deep 
moisture/decaying Atmospheric River entering the southwestern US 
tonight. Some of the moisture will rapidly push northeastward as a 
deep trough lifts across the Rockies and a Colorado low forms 
tomorrow night. The storm track will be quite amplified/stay well to 
our west through midweek and anomalous moisture stays to our north. 
Trends have continued to suggest that the polar jet gets absorbed 
into this system by Tuesday morning while high pressure builds back 
over our region following slightly enhanced gradient flow on Monday. 

However, frontal forcing for light rain may make its closest 
approach Tuesday afternoon, as some low level moisture gets pulled 
northward around the ridge of high pressure centered over the 
western mid-Atlantic region to support increasing rain chances. In 
any case, where clouds wind up being thick and persistent, 
temperatures will end up being a bit lower than currently forecast. 
Greatest chances of the cooler/cloudier scenario is over the 
northern St. Lawrence Valley, and secondarily across north 
central/northeastern Vermont and the remainder of northern New York. 
Otherwise, most likely highs both Monday and Tuesday will be about 
10 to 15 degrees above normal in the upper 50s to mid 60s.

KEY MESSAGE 2: The next significant weather maker will be a large 
trough / cold front late next week. Models are coming into agreement 
that the trough will come off the Rocky Mountains on Tuesday or 
Wednesday and begin to develop into a large area of low pressure 
over the Plains. The timing and intensity of this front remains 
highly questionable, as it will need to work around a ridge of high 
pressure off the Atlantic Coast. The current thinking is we'll see 
winds ramp up on Wednesday and Thursday as the pressure gradient 
between the ridge and trough tightens. The setup favors channeled 
flow into the Champlain Valley, with southerly winds bringing gusts 
up to 30mph. The main low pressure system will then slide into the 
northeast sometime between Friday and next Sunday. The GFS solution 
has the low moving quicker, with less intensity while the Euro is 
showing the low becoming more pronounced and bringing precipitation 
to northern New York and Vermont through Sunday. We do have some 
time before the impacts arrive and will continue to update the 
forecast as the forecast comes into focus.
